SuperComputer

By: Siniketiwe Hlanze | Production

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
We uncover the new era of computing

Unique Selling Point:
Global conglomerates are competing to against each other to create the world's super computer. IBM and Wits have started a programme where researchers from around the continent can explore how the science of quantum computing can help bring solutions to their respective fields. Although IBM's supercomputer is kept in New York, the piece will have voices of scientists that will speak about its potential for various research problems for health and other issues as well as the new era of science.

Summary:
Exploring quantum computing and its potential at a time when buzzwords like AI and 4IR are touted as being the peak examples of science and technology.

Further information:
IBM's Quantum computer is based in New Yorker as it should be kept under very cold temperatures. Footage of it will be sourced from IBM.

Script:


VO
Upsound
Visuals
The evolution of computers over time has been one of technology’s marvels.
From the very first computer in the 40s, the first commercially viable desktop and modern times smart devices.



OPENING LINK: Imagine a world of advanced super computers where all that we know about coding and programming is being turned on its head. We are on the cusp of a new era and it's got some of the world's top researchers excited. Welcome to quantum computing





Quantum Computer Chandelier
VO: Quantum computing refers to an advanced system with much greater processing power. Through a partnership between global I.T company IBM and Wits University – experts in Johannesburg are at the forefront of this innovation

IBM Introductory Link:
Dr Ismail Akhalwaya is part of the team at IBM Africa that is exploring ways to practically apply quantum computing in fields such as commerce, health and science



VO: An actual quantum computer looks like a chandelier with a tiny chip at the bottom. The chip holds its processing power. There’s only a few of these around the world and are kept under stringent conditions


Masa: What makes the quantum computer special:
Quantum mechanics is a theory of the physical universe and it’s got some very strange properties, and those properties are being harnessed for computing. Those properties, three of them involve, super positioning which means multiple states at the same time, entanglement which means a coupling of those states and interference which means those states affect each other. And low and behold out of these three properties of quantum mechanics, we can do computing.



Masa: Tell me about the Chandelier
Ismail: We call it the chandelier cause its so pretty. It hangs in the fridge, under vacuum so all the air is sucked out and its cooled to minus 273 degree celsius, a sliver above absolute zero. The wires you see are the communication channels and we have to take the information from the normal temperature to the super cold world at these cold temperatures we have better control over the weirdness of quantum mechanics and then we read out the information after we have computed on it.


FACT: Absolute zero is -273.15 C

VO:Quantum computers will allow experts and academics in different fields to pioneer new research and push the boundaries of what is possible
For Conrad Haupt - an electrical engineering masters student - this presents new ways of problem solving



Conrad
there are certain problems that are too large, not necessarily big data, not necessarily with too many variables but ones which are too complex for normal computers/classical computers that we’ll be able to solve, the analogy is that quantum computers have multiple hands and so can go through multiple answers.


VO: Waheeda Saib, health scientist at IBM says using quantum computers will help shorten the time to development of new drugs.



09:19 A classical computer we can only use it to process information or instruction sequentially and for a quantum computer you can process information simultaneously, so that means for example in drug discovery. On a quantum computer we can actually represent to the better, higher degree the molecules required to actually look for better drugs and also we can do drug repurposing for example malaria we can find drugs that are actually similar to the ones that have become drug resistant so we can try that, we can also find eh search a greater eh new anti-biotics.
